l: Cardiovascular System - Lecture 3
Department of Physiology
Second Year Medicine
- Describe the conduction system of the heart
- Explain the phases of the cardiac cycle
- Calculate cardiac output and explain how it is regulated
- The heart has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it out.
- The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk; the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta.
- The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than that of the right ventricle because it pumps against a higher pressure.
- The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle; the mitral (bicuspid) valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle.
- The pulmonary and aortic valves are semilunar valves that prevent backflow from the arteries into the ventricles.
- Cardiac muscle cells are striated, branched and usually have one central nucleus.
- Intercalated discs join neighbouring cells; their gap junctions let action potentials spread from cell to cell.
- Desmosomes in the intercalated discs hold the cells together during contraction.
- Cardiac muscle has a long refractory period, so it cannot be tetanized.
- The sinoatrial (SA) node in the wall of the right atrium is the normal pacemaker of the heart.
- The impulse spreads through the atrial muscle to the atrioventricular (AV) node.
- The AV node delays the impulse by about 0.1 second, so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles contract.
- From the AV node the impulse passes to the bundle of His, the right and left bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibres.
- Purkinje fibres conduct the impulse fastest and spread it through the ventricular muscle from the apex upward.
- SA node cells have no stable resting potential; they depolarize slowly toward threshold.
- The slow depolarization is caused by the funny current (If), an inward sodium current through HCN channels.
- At threshold, calcium enters through L-type calcium channels and produces the upstroke of the action potential.
- Repolarization is caused by the opening of potassium channels.
- Phase 0: rapid depolarization as fast voltage-gated sodium channels open.
- Phase 1: brief early repolarization as the sodium channels inactivate and transient potassium channels open.
- Phase 2: the plateau, in which calcium entry through L-type channels balances potassium exit.
- Phase 3: repolarization as the calcium channels close and potassium efflux increases.
- Phase 4: the resting membrane potential of about -90 mV.
- The P wave represents atrial depolarization.
- The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization; atrial repolarization is hidden within it.
- The T wave represents ventricular repolarization.
- The PR interval, normally 0.12 to 0.20 second, reflects conduction from the atria through the AV node.
- A QRS complex longer than 0.12 second suggests delayed conduction within the ventricles.
- Atrial systole pushes the last 20 to 30% of ventricular filling into the ventricles.
- Isovolumetric contraction begins when the atrioventricular valves close; all four valves are closed and the ventricular volume does not change.
- Ventricular ejection begins when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and the semilunar valves open.
- Isovolumetric relaxation begins when the semilunar valves close; ventricular pressure falls while all valves are closed.
- Ventricular filling begins when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure and the atrioventricular valves open.
- The first heart sound (S1) is caused by closure of the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole.
- The second heart sound (S2) is caused by closure of the semilunar valves at the start of ventricular diastole.
- A third heart sound (S3) may be heard during rapid ventricular filling and is normal in children.
- Murmurs are abnormal sounds caused by turbulent blood flow, for example through a narrowed (stenotic) valve.
- Cardiac output is the volume of blood each ventricle pumps per minute: cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.
- At rest, a heart rate of 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL give a cardiac output of about 4.9 litres per minute.
- Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume - end-systolic volume, for example 120 mL - 50 mL = 70 mL.
- Ejection fraction = stroke volume / end-diastolic volume; it is normally about 55 to 70%.
- Preload is the degree of stretch of the ventricular muscle before contraction; it rises when venous return rises.
- Frank-Starling law: the greater the stretch of the ventricle in diastole, the stronger its contraction and the larger the stroke volume.
- Contractility is the force of contraction at a given preload; sympathetic stimulation increases it.
- Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome to eject blood; a high arterial pressure increases afterload and reduces stroke volume.
- Sympathetic nerves release noradrenaline, which acts on beta-1 receptors to increase heart rate and contractility.
- Parasympathetic fibres of the vagus nerve release acetylcholine, which acts on M2 receptors to slow the heart rate.
- At rest the vagus nerve dominates, so the resting heart rate is lower than the intrinsic SA node rate of about 100 beats per minute.
- Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla, a high body temperature and thyroid hormone also increase heart rate.
1. A patient's heart rate is 80 beats per minute and the stroke volume is 60 mL. What is the cardiac output?
2. Which valves close at the start of isovolumetric contraction?

Pharmacology - Lecture 8
College of Pharmacy
- Classify antibacterial drugs by their target
- Describe the mechanism, uses and adverse effects of the main classes
- Explain the mechanisms of bacterial resistance
- Bactericidal drugs kill bacteria, whereas bacteriostatic drugs stop their growth and rely on the host's immune system to clear the infection.
- The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest drug concentration that prevents visible bacterial growth.
- Broad-spectrum antibiotics act on many Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria; narrow-spectrum antibiotics act on a limited group.
- Selective toxicity means the drug harms the microbe more than the host, usually by targeting a structure that host cells lack.
- Cell wall synthesis: beta-lactams and vancomycin.
- Protein synthesis: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines and macrolides.
- Nucleic acid synthesis: fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV.
- Folate synthesis: sulfonamides and trimethoprim block two successive steps of folic acid synthesis.
- Beta-lactams include penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams; all contain a beta-lactam ring.
- They bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall.
- Their action is bactericidal and greatest on dividing bacteria.
- The most important adverse effect of penicillins is hypersensitivity, ranging from a rash to anaphylaxis.
- Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) is given by injection because it is destroyed by stomach acid.
- Amoxicillin has a broader spectrum that includes some Gram-negative bacteria, and it is well absorbed orally.
- Flucloxacillin resists staphylococcal penicillinase and is used for penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus aureus.
- Clavulanic acid inhibits beta-lactamase; combined with amoxicillin it protects amoxicillin from destruction.
- Cephalosporins are grouped into generations; later generations have greater activity against Gram-negative bacteria.
- Ceftriaxone, a third-generation cephalosporin, reaches the cerebrospinal fluid and is used in bacterial meningitis.
- Carbapenems such as meropenem have the broadest spectrum of the beta-lactams and resist most beta-lactamases.
- A small proportion of patients allergic to penicillin (about 1 to 2%) also react to cephalosporins.
- Vancomycin is a glycopeptide that binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell wall synthesis.
- It acts only on Gram-positive bacteria and is used for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
- Rapid infusion can cause flushing of the upper body, known as red man syndrome.
- It can damage the kidneys and the inner ear, so its blood levels are monitored.
- Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and cause misreading of messenger RNA.
- They are bactericidal and act mainly on aerobic Gram-negative bacteria.
- They are not absorbed from the gut and are given by injection.
- Their main toxic effects are nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
- Tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit and block the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA; they are bacteriostatic.
- Tetracyclines bind calcium and stain developing teeth, so they are avoided in children under eight years and in pregnancy.
- Macrolides such as erythromycin and azithromycin bind the 50S subunit and block the elongation of the peptide chain.
- Macrolides are an alternative for patients allergic to penicillin; erythromycin often causes gastrointestinal upset.
- Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV and are bactericidal.
- They are well absorbed orally, but antacids containing calcium or magnesium reduce their absorption.
- Their adverse effects include damage to tendons, with a risk of tendon rupture, especially in older adults.
- Enzymatic inactivation: beta-lactamases hydrolyse the beta-lactam ring.
- Altered target: MRSA produces PBP2a, which has a low affinity for beta-lactams.
- Reduced entry or active efflux: the loss of porins and efflux pumps lower the drug concentration inside the cell.
- Resistance genes can spread between bacteria on plasmids by conjugation.
1. A patient with MRSA infection needs treatment. Which drug from this lecture would you choose, and why?
2. Why is gentamicin not given by mouth?

Immunology - Lecture 2
Faculty of Medicine
- Compare innate and adaptive immunity
- Describe inflammation, phagocytosis and complement
- Describe the roles of T cells, B cells and antibodies
- Innate immunity is present from birth, responds within minutes to hours and does not improve with repeated exposure.
- Adaptive immunity takes days to develop, is specific to each antigen and forms immunological memory.
- The first line of defence consists of physical and chemical barriers such as intact skin, mucus and stomach acid.
- Neutrophils are the most numerous white blood cells and the first phagocytes to arrive at a site of infection.
- Macrophages develop from monocytes that leave the blood; they phagocytose microbes and present antigens.
- Natural killer (NK) cells kill virus-infected cells and tumour cells without prior sensitization.
- Mast cells release histamine, which increases vascular permeability.
- The cardinal signs of inflammation are redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function.
- Histamine and other mediators dilate arterioles and make capillaries more permeable, so fluid and proteins leak into the tissue.
- Neutrophils reach the tissue in steps: margination, rolling along the endothelium, firm adhesion, then migration through the vessel wall (diapedesis).
- Neutrophils then move toward the site of infection by chemotaxis.
- The steps of phagocytosis are chemotaxis, adherence to the microbe, ingestion into a phagosome, fusion with a lysosome, and killing and digestion.
- Opsonins such as the complement fragment C3b and IgG antibodies coat microbes and make them easier to ingest.
- Phagocytes kill ingested microbes with reactive oxygen species produced by the respiratory burst.
- The classical pathway is activated by antibodies bound to an antigen.
- The alternative pathway is activated directly on microbial surfaces.
- The lectin pathway is activated when mannose-binding lectin binds sugars on microbes.
- All three pathways meet at the cleavage of C3: C3b acts as an opsonin, C3a and C5a attract inflammatory cells, and C5b to C9 form the membrane attack complex that lyses cells.
- MHC class I molecules are found on all nucleated cells and present peptides from inside the cell to CD8+ T cells.
- MHC class II molecules are found on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells) and present peptides to CD4+ T cells.
- Dendritic cells are the most effective antigen-presenting cells for activating naive T cells.
- T cells mature in the thymus.
- Helper T cells (CD4+) release cytokines that activate B cells, macrophages and cytotoxic T cells.
- Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) kill virus-infected cells by releasing perforin and granzymes.
- Regulatory T cells suppress immune responses and help to prevent autoimmunity.
- B cells mature in the bone marrow; when activated they become plasma cells that secrete antibodies.
- IgM is the first antibody produced in a primary response and exists as a pentamer.
- IgG is the most abundant antibody in serum and the only one that crosses the placenta.
- IgA is found in secretions such as saliva, tears and breast milk; IgE binds mast cells and mediates allergic reactions.
- In the primary response antibodies appear after a lag of about 7 to 10 days, and IgM predominates.
- In the secondary response memory cells produce more antibody, faster, and mainly IgG.
- Vaccination produces memory cells without causing the disease.
- Active immunity is produced by the person's own immune system after infection or vaccination, and it lasts a long time.
- Passive immunity is the transfer of ready-made antibodies, such as maternal IgG across the placenta or an injection of antiserum.
- Passive immunity acts immediately but lasts only weeks to months, because no memory cells are formed.
- Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity is mediated by IgE on mast cells; an example is anaphylaxis.
- Type II is caused by antibodies against cell-surface antigens; an example is a transfusion reaction.
- Type III is caused by immune complexes deposited in tissues; an example is serum sickness.
- Type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity is mediated by T cells and appears after 48 to 72 hours; an example is the tuberculin skin test.
1. Which antibody would you measure to detect a recent infection, and why?
2. Why does a baby have protection against some infections in its first months?
Physiology - Lecture 6
Department of Physiology
- Explain the mechanics of breathing
- Describe gas exchange and the transport of gases
- Describe the control of breathing
- During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs.
- The thoracic volume increases, so the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in.
- Quiet expiration is passive: the muscles relax and the elastic recoil of the lungs pushes air out.
- Tidal volume, the air moved in one quiet breath, is about 500 mL.
- Residual volume, the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiration, is about 1200 mL.
- Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inspiration.
- Total lung capacity is the vital capacity plus the residual volume.
- Surfactant is secreted by type II alveolar cells and lowers the surface tension in the alveoli.
- Without surfactant the alveoli tend to collapse, as in the respiratory distress syndrome of premature infants.
- Compliance describes how easily the lungs stretch; it is reduced in pulmonary fibrosis.
- Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the respiratory membrane by simple diffusion, down their partial pressure gradients.
- The partial pressure of oxygen is about 100 mmHg in the alveoli and about 40 mmHg in the venous blood that reaches the lungs.
- Carbon dioxide diffuses about 20 times faster than oxygen because it is more soluble.
- About 98.5% of the oxygen in blood is carried bound to haemoglobin; the rest is dissolved in plasma.
- Each haemoglobin molecule can bind four oxygen molecules.
- A rise in carbon dioxide, acidity or temperature shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, so more oxygen is released to the tissues (the Bohr effect).
- About 70% of carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate ions, about 23% bound to haemoglobin and about 7% dissolved in plasma.
- In red blood cells carbonic anhydrase combines carbon dioxide and water into carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate.
- The respiratory centres are in the medulla oblongata and the pons.
- Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond mainly to a rise in carbon dioxide, sensed as a fall in the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid.
- Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond when arterial oxygen falls below about 60 mmHg.

Microbiology - Lecture 4
Department of Medical Microbiology
- Describe the bacterial growth curve
- Classify bacteria by their temperature and oxygen needs
- Describe common culture media
- Bacteria reproduce by binary fission: one cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
- Generation time is the time a population needs to double; for Escherichia coli under ideal conditions it is about 20 minutes.
- Lag phase: the cells adapt to the new medium and make enzymes, but their number hardly changes.
- Log (exponential) phase: the cells divide at a constant, maximal rate and are most sensitive to antibiotics.
- Stationary phase: nutrients run out and waste builds up, so the number of new cells equals the number of dying cells.
- Death phase: the number of living cells declines.
- Psychrophiles grow best below about 15 degrees Celsius.
- Mesophiles grow best between about 20 and 45 degrees Celsius; most human pathogens are mesophiles with an optimum near 37 degrees.
- Thermophiles grow best above about 45 degrees Celsius.
- Obligate aerobes require oxygen for growth.
- Obligate anaerobes are killed by oxygen; Clostridium species are examples.
- Facultative anaerobes grow with or without oxygen but grow better with it; Escherichia coli is an example.
- Microaerophiles need oxygen at a lower concentration than in air.
- Selective media contain substances that inhibit some organisms and let others grow.
- Differential media let different organisms be told apart by their appearance, such as the colour of their colonies.
- MacConkey agar is both selective and differential: it inhibits Gram-positive bacteria and separates lactose fermenters (pink colonies) from non-fermenters.
- On blood agar, beta-haemolysis is a clear zone around the colony, alpha-haemolysis a greenish zone, and gamma means no haemolysis.
- A viable plate count counts only living cells and reports colony-forming units (CFU).
- Turbidity measured with a spectrophotometer estimates living and dead cells together.
1. In which phase would an antibiotic that acts on the cell wall work best?
2. Pink colonies grow on MacConkey agar. What do they tell you?
Fundamentals of Nursing - Week 5
School of Nursing
- Describe the chain of infection
- Apply standard and transmission-based precautions
- Put on and remove personal protective equipment in the correct order
- The six links are the infectious agent, the reservoir, the portal of exit, the mode of transmission, the portal of entry and the susceptible host.
- Breaking any one link prevents the spread of infection.
- Contact transmission is direct, from person to person, or indirect, through a contaminated object called a fomite.
- Droplet transmission involves large particles that travel less than about one metre, for example in influenza.
- Airborne transmission involves small particles that stay suspended in the air, for example in tuberculosis and measles.
- Hand hygiene is the single most important measure for preventing healthcare-associated infections.
- An alcohol-based hand rub is preferred when the hands are not visibly soiled; it takes about 20 to 30 seconds.
- Hands must be washed with soap and water when they are visibly soiled and after caring for a patient with Clostridioides difficile, because alcohol does not kill its spores.

- The WHO five moments are: before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after a risk of body fluid exposure, after touching a patient, and after touching the patient's surroundings.
- Standard precautions apply to all patients, whatever their diagnosis.
- They include hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, safe injection practices, respiratory hygiene and the safe handling of sharps.
- Used needles are never recapped; they go directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container.
- Contact precautions: a gown and gloves when entering the room, for example for MRSA.
- Droplet precautions: a surgical mask within about one metre of the patient, for example for influenza.
- Airborne precautions: an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room, for example for tuberculosis.
- PPE is put on in this order: gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, then gloves.
- PPE is removed in this order: gloves, goggles or face shield, gown, then mask or respirator.
- Hand hygiene is performed immediately after all PPE is removed.
1. A patient has pulmonary tuberculosis. Which precautions does the nurse use?
2. Which item of PPE is removed first?

Biology 101 - Lecture 1
- The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.
- It is selectively permeable: it controls what enters and leaves the cell.
- The nucleus contains the cell's DNA.
- The nucleolus inside the nucleus makes ribosomal RNA.
- Ribosomes make proteins.
- The rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes on its surface and makes proteins for export.
- The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins.
- Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP by aerobic respiration.
- Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down worn-out organelles.
- The smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes lipids and detoxifies drugs.
Health Sciences - Lecture 2
- Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the macronutrients.
- Carbohydrates and proteins provide about 4 kcal per gram; fats provide about 9 kcal per gram.
- Proteins are made of amino acids.
- Essential amino acids cannot be made by the body and must come from food.
- Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and can be stored in the body.
- Vitamin C and the B vitamins are water-soluble.
- Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
- Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; iron deficiency causes anaemia.
- Water makes up about 60% of an adult's body weight.
